# Second Law of Thermodynamics {#sec-ch5}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Explain key concepts related to the second law of thermodynamics (e.g.
  **heat engines**, **refrigerators** and **heat pumps**).
- State the second law of thermodynamics in two different forms.
- Evaluate the performance of thermodynamic cycles (i.e. **thermal
  efficiency**).
:::

## Introduction

The second law of thermodynamics is one of the most important laws of nature.
It distinguishes between work and heat. It also acknowledges that spontaneous
processes proceed in certain directions.

![A hot body left in the atmosphere cools down to $T_0$, and air at high pressure escapes through an opened valve until it reaches $p_0$. Both processes happen by themselves from left to right; neither ever runs back from right to left on its own.](figures/out/ch5-spontaneous.svg){width=88%}

The First Law would be perfectly satisfied if the body in the figure took heat
back from the atmosphere and warmed up again, or if the air flowed back into the
tank: energy would still be conserved. It is the **Second Law** that tells us
these reverse processes do not happen by themselves.

## Heat engines

A **heat engine** is a system that operates in a *cycle* and *delivers work* at
the expense of *receiving heat* from the surroundings. In our sign convention, a
heat engine therefore has a net work output, $W < 0$, and a net heat input,
$Q > 0$.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![](figures/out/ch5-power-plant.svg)

![](figures/img/ch5-power-plant-photo.png)
:::

A steam power plant is a heat engine. Heat is received in the boiler
($\dot{Q}_\text{boiler} > 0$), heat is rejected in the condenser
($\dot{Q}_\text{con} < 0$), and the turbine delivers the net work
($\dot{W} < 0$). Part of the work produced by the turbine is used, through the
shaft, to drive the pump.

Any heat engine can be represented by the same simple picture: it receives heat
$Q_H$ from a **hot reservoir**, delivers work $W$, and rejects heat $Q_C$ to a
**cold reservoir**.

![](figures/out/ch5-heat-engine.svg){width=36% fig-align="center"}

Applying the First Law to the cycle of a heat engine:

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="First Law for a cycle, $\sum Q + \sum W = 0$: the heats are $Q_H$ and $Q_C$, the work is $W$."}
$$
\sum Q + \sum W = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
Q_H + Q_C + W = 0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="Signs: $Q_H > 0$, $Q_C < 0$, $W < 0$. Rewrite in magnitudes."}
With $Q_H > 0$, $Q_C < 0$ and $W < 0$, in terms of magnitudes:
$$
|Q_H| - |Q_C| - |W| = 0
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
|Q_H| - |Q_C| = |W|
$$ {#eq-ch5-engine}
:::

### Thermal efficiency

In general, **efficiency** is the ratio of output, the energy sought, to input,
the energy that costs. For a *heat engine*, the thermal efficiency is given by:

$$
\eta = \frac{\text{energy sought}}{\text{energy that costs}}
$$

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Sought: the work out, $|W|$. Costs: the heat in, $|Q_H|$ (the fuel)."}
$$
\eta = \frac{|W|}{|Q_H|}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="Replace $|W|$ using $|W| = |Q_H| - |Q_C|$."}
Using @eq-ch5-engine, $|W| = |Q_H| - |Q_C|$:
$$
\eta = \frac{|Q_H| - |Q_C|}{|Q_H|} = 1 - \frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\eta = \frac{|W|}{|Q_H|} = 1 - \frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|}
$$ {#eq-ch5-eta}
:::

::: {.example}
An automobile engine produces a power of 100 kW on the output shaft with a
thermal efficiency of 30%. Find (i) the rate of energy received by burning fuel
in the engine, (ii) the rate of energy rejected to the ambient.

![](figures/img/ch5-car.png){width=40% fig-align="center"}

**Step 1.** *The energy received from the fuel is the heat input to the engine.
Which quantity in @eq-ch5-eta is it, and which one is the 100 kW?*

::: {.gap height="22mm" hint="Energy from burning fuel $= |\dot{Q}_H|$; $\eta = 100/|\dot{Q}_H| = 0.3$, so $|\dot{Q}_H| = 333.3$ kW."}
The rate of energy received by burning fuel is $|\dot{Q}_H|$, and the shaft
power is $|\dot{W}|$:
$$
\eta = \frac{|\dot{W}|}{|\dot{Q}_H|} = \frac{100~\mathrm{kW}}{|\dot{Q}_H|} = 0.3
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\boxed{|\dot{Q}_H| = 333.3~\mathrm{kW}}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *The energy rejected to the ambient is $|\dot{Q}_C|$. Use the First
Law for the engine.*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$|\dot{Q}_C| = |\dot{Q}_H| - |\dot{W}| = 333.3 - 100 = 233.3$ kW."}
$$
|\dot{Q}_C| = |\dot{Q}_H| - |\dot{W}| = 333.3 - 100
= \boxed{233.3~\mathrm{kW}}
$$
:::
:::

## Second Law of thermodynamics

The Second Law of thermodynamics can be stated as below, which is known as the
***Kelvin–Planck statement***:

::: {.key}
*"It is impossible for any system to operate in a thermodynamic cycle and
deliver a net amount of work to its surroundings while receiving heat from a
single reservoir."*
:::

![Max Planck (1858–1947) and the Lord Kelvin (1824–1907).](figures/img/ch5-planck-kelvin.png){width=34%}

::: {.note}
The second law of thermodynamics (like every other law of nature) rests on
***experimental evidence***, and it *cannot* be proved.
:::

![An engine that exchanges heat with a single reservoir and delivers work is impossible: some heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir, $|Q_C| \neq 0$.](figures/img/ch5-kp-impossible.png){width=32%}

::: {.note}
From the Second Law, the efficiency of a heat engine is always less than unity,
and some heat must always be rejected during the cycle:
$$
\eta = \frac{|W|}{|Q_H|} < 1
$$
:::

::: {.note}
According to the second law, it is still possible to have a cycle that converts
all of the *work input* into *heat energy output*.

![](figures/out/ch5-work-heat.svg){width=80% fig-align="center"}

The reverse is not possible: the work output of a cycle is always less than
its heat input, $W_\text{output} < Q_\text{input}$.
:::

In a cycle, heat can never be converted entirely into work, but work can always
be converted into heat. This is often expressed as "***work is a more valuable
form of energy transfer than heat***".

## Corollary one: Clausius statement of the Second Law

::: {.key}
*"It is **impossible** to construct a system that operates in a cycle and
transfer **heat from a cooler to a hotter body without work** being done on the
system by the surroundings."*
:::

::: {layout="[[22,-8,50,-20]]"}
![](figures/img/ch5-clausius.png)

![](figures/out/ch5-clausius-bars.svg)
:::

Heat flows through a metal bar from the hot to the cold body by itself. To move
heat from the cold to the hot body, work must be done on the system, $W > 0$.

::: {.note}
The two statements of the second law, namely the *Kelvin–Planck* and the
*Clausius* statements, are *equivalent*. This means that the violation of one
implies the violation of the other.
:::

## Refrigerators and heat pumps

In both *refrigerators* and *heat pumps*, heat is transferred *from* a **cold**
reservoir *to* a **hot** reservoir. According to the second law, work has to be
done on the system to make this happen.

::: {layout="[[22,-6,60,-12]]"}
![](figures/img/ch5-fridge.png)

![](figures/img/ch5-ac-heat-pump.png)
:::

| Device | Cold reservoir | Hot reservoir |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Refrigerator | the inside of the fridge | the kitchen |
| Air conditioner (summer) | the inside of the house | the outside air |
| Heat pump (winter) | the outside air | the inside of the house |

In each case heat is taken from the cold reservoir, $Q_C > 0$, and rejected to
the hot reservoir, $Q_H < 0$, and the device needs a work input, $W > 0$ (in a
refrigerator, the electrical work that drives the compressor).

![](figures/out/ch5-refrigerator.svg){width=40% fig-align="center"}

Applying the First Law to the cycle, now with $Q_H < 0$, $Q_C > 0$ and
$W > 0$:

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="$Q_H + Q_C + W = 0$ with $Q_H < 0$, $Q_C > 0$, $W > 0$; write in magnitudes."}
$$
Q_H + Q_C + W = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
-|Q_H| + |Q_C| + |W| = 0
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
|Q_H| = |Q_C| + |W|
$$ {#eq-ch5-fridge}
:::

::: {.note}
A **refrigerator** is a **cooling** system, so its primary objective is the
amount of heat transferred from the cold environment. In contrast, a **heat
pump** is a **heating** system, so its primary objective is the heat
transferred to the hot environment.
:::

**Refrigerator:** the performance of a refrigerator is expressed in terms of the
**coefficient of performance (COP)**, shown by the symbol $\beta$.

$$
\beta = \frac{\text{energy sought}}{\text{energy that costs}}
$$

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Sought: the heat taken out of the cold space, $|Q_C|$. Costs: the work, $|W|$."}
$$
\beta = \frac{|Q_C|}{|W|}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="Replace $|Q_C|$ using $|Q_C| = |Q_H| - |W|$."}
Using @eq-ch5-fridge, $|Q_C| = |Q_H| - |W|$:
$$
\beta = \frac{|Q_H| - |W|}{|W|} = \frac{|Q_H|}{|W|} - 1
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\beta = \frac{|Q_C|}{|W|} = \frac{|Q_H|}{|W|} - 1
$$ {#eq-ch5-beta}
:::

::: {.note}
According to the second law, the COP of a refrigerator is always less than
infinity, $0 < \beta < \infty$. In reality, a household refrigerator may have a
COP of about 2.5.
:::

**Heat pump:** the COP for a heat pump is denoted by $\beta'$ and is given by

$$
\beta' = \frac{\text{energy sought}}{\text{energy that costs}}
$$

::: {.gap height="18mm" hint="Sought: the heat delivered to the hot space, $|Q_H|$. Costs: the work, $|W|$."}
$$
\beta' = \frac{|Q_H|}{|W|}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="Replace $|Q_H|$ using $|Q_H| = |Q_C| + |W|$, and spot $\beta$."}
Using @eq-ch5-fridge, $|Q_H| = |Q_C| + |W|$:
$$
\beta' = \frac{|Q_C| + |W|}{|W|} = \underbrace{\frac{|Q_C|}{|W|}}_{\beta} + 1
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
\beta' = \frac{|Q_H|}{|W|} = \beta + 1
$$ {#eq-ch5-betap}
:::

::: {.example}
The refrigerator in a kitchen receives electrical power of 150 W, and it rejects
400 W to the kitchen air. Find the rate of energy taken out of the cold space
inside the refrigerator and the COP of the refrigerator.

![](figures/img/ch5-fridge.png){width=22% fig-align="center"}

**Step 1.** *Which of $|\dot{Q}_H|$, $|\dot{Q}_C|$ and $|\dot{W}|$ are given?
Use the First Law for the refrigerator.*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$|\dot{W}| = 150$ W, $|\dot{Q}_H| = 400$ W; $|\dot{Q}_C| = 400 - 150 = 250$ W."}
The electrical power is the work input, $|\dot{W}| = 150$ W, and the heat
rejected to the kitchen is $|\dot{Q}_H| = 400$ W. From the First Law:
$$
|\dot{Q}_C| = |\dot{Q}_H| - |\dot{W}| = 400 - 150 = \boxed{250~\mathrm{W}}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *Now the COP, from @eq-ch5-beta.*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$\beta = |\dot{Q}_C|/|\dot{W}| = 250/150 = 1.67$."}
$$
\beta = \frac{|\dot{Q}_C|}{|\dot{W}|} = \frac{250}{150} = \boxed{1.67}
$$
:::
:::

## Reversible cycle

If **every** process in the cycle is *reversible*, then the whole cycle is
**reversible**.

::: {.note}
**Reminder:** a process is *reversible* if both the system and its surroundings
can be exactly restored to their initial states.
:::

If a reversible heat engine cycle is reversed, it becomes a refrigerator with
the exact same magnitude of heat transfers and work.

![](figures/out/ch5-reverse.svg){width=86% fig-align="center"}

### Common sources of irreversibility

1. **Unrestrained expansion.** A gas that expands suddenly into a vacuum, or
   against a much lower pressure (like the air escaping through the valve in
   the introduction), does no useful work, and it cannot be pushed back into
   its original volume without work being done by the surroundings.
2. **Heat transfer through a finite temperature difference.** Heat flows by
   itself from a hotter to a colder body (like the hot body cooling in the
   introduction). By the Clausius statement, it cannot be sent back without
   work being done.
3. **Friction.** Friction turns work into heat, and by the Kelvin–Planck
   statement that heat can never be turned entirely back into work.

::: {.note}
Since at least one of the sources of irreversibility discussed above is always
present in some degree, no real process can be reversible. The reversible
process (and a reversible cycle) must therefore be regarded as a limiting case
– an ideal that can never quite be achieved.
:::

## Explore it yourself {#sec-ch5-explore}

A heat engine, a refrigerator and a heat pump all work in a cycle between a hot
and a cold reservoir. The first law fixes how the energy flows add up; the
second law says which of these devices can exist.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Choose a device and move the sliders. Which energy is *sought* and which one
*costs*? Then try to build an engine with $\eta = 100\%$, or a refrigerator
that needs no work. Which statement of the second law does each one break?

## End-of-chapter problems {#sec-ch5-problems}

::: {.tryfirst}
Have a real go at every problem here before you look at its solution. All the
worked solutions are available from the start (under each problem on the
website, and in the completed notes), so the only thing between you and a
solution is your own decision to wait. Use it well: reading a solution is not
the same as being able to produce one, and the time you spend stuck on a
problem is where most of the learning happens. Only once you have an answer of
your own, or have tried every approach you can think of, check it against the
solution, and compare the method, not just the final number.
:::


**P5.1 [easy].** A heat engine operates continuously and receives energy by heat
transfer from the combustion of fuel at a rate of 75 kW. If the thermal
efficiency of the cycle is 33%, at what rate is power developed, in kW?

**(a)** 24.75 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 33 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 10.6 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 36.9

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.hint}
Use the definition of thermal efficiency: which energy rate does the fuel provide?
:::

::: {.answer}
$|\dot{W}_\text{net}| = 24.75$ kW, option **(a)**.
:::

::: {.worked}
The heat engine receives $|\dot{Q}_H| = 75$ kW and delivers the net power
$|\dot{W}_\text{net}|$, rejecting $\dot{Q}_C$ to the cold reservoir. To find
the rate of power developed we need $|\dot{W}_\text{net}|$:
$$
\eta = \frac{|\dot{W}_\text{net}|}{|\dot{Q}_H|} = 0.33
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|\dot{W}_\text{net}| = 0.33 \times 75~\mathrm{kW}
= \boxed{24.75~\mathrm{kW}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P5.2 [easy].** A heat engine operates with a thermal efficiency of 28%. If heat
extracted by the engine from the hot reservoir is 600 kJ, how much heat was
rejected into the cold reservoir, in kJ?

**(a)** 368 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 168 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 600 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 432

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.hint}
First law for the cycle plus the definition of efficiency. Careful: the question asks for the heat rejected, not the work.
:::

::: {.answer}
$|Q_C| = 432$ kJ, option **(d)**.
:::

::: {.worked}
The thermal efficiency of a heat engine is given by
$$
\eta = \frac{|W|}{|Q_H|} = \frac{|Q_H| - |Q_C|}{|Q_H|}
     = 1 - \frac{|Q_C|}{|Q_H|} = 0.28,
\qquad |Q_H| = 600~\mathrm{kJ}
$$
$$
\Rightarrow\quad
|Q_C| = (1 - 0.28) \times 600~\mathrm{kJ}
= \boxed{432~\mathrm{kJ}} \quad \text{(d)}
$$
:::
:::

**P5.3 [easy].** The coefficient of performance of a heat pump cycle is 3.
Calculate the heat removed from the cold reservoir if 12 kW of heat was
supplied to the hot reservoir.

**(a)** 4 kW &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 8 kW &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 12 kW &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 3 kW

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.hint}
Use the heat-pump COP (not the refrigerator one), then the first law for the cycle.
:::

::: {.answer}
$|\dot{Q}_C| = 8$ kW, option **(b)**.
:::

::: {.worked}
The COP for a heat pump is given by
$$
\beta' = \frac{|\dot{Q}_H|}{|\dot{W}|}
       = \frac{|\dot{Q}_H|}{|\dot{Q}_H| - |\dot{Q}_C|} = 3,
\qquad |\dot{Q}_H| = 12~\mathrm{kW}
$$
$$
\Rightarrow\quad
3\left(12~\mathrm{kW} - |\dot{Q}_C|\right) = 12~\mathrm{kW}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\boxed{|\dot{Q}_C| = 8~\mathrm{kW}} \quad \text{(b)}
$$
:::
:::

**P5.4 [easy].** A refrigerator removes 1.5 kJ from the cold space using 1 kJ
work input. How much energy goes into the kitchen, and what is its coefficient
of performance?

![](figures/img/ch5-p-fridge.png){width=20%}

**(a)** 2.5 kJ, 1.5 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 3.5 kJ, 3 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** 0.5 kJ, 1 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 1 kJ, 2

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.hint}
First law for the cycle. For the COP: what is the useful effect of a refrigerator?
:::

::: {.answer}
$|Q_H| = 2.5$ kJ and $\beta = 1.5$, option **(a)**.
:::

::: {.worked}
Here $|Q_C| = 1.5$ kJ and $|W| = 1$ kJ; $Q_H$ is unknown. From the energy
equation:
$$
|Q_H| = |W| + |Q_C| = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5~\mathrm{kJ}
$$

COP:
$$
\beta = \frac{|Q_C|}{|W|} = \frac{1.5~\mathrm{kJ}}{1~\mathrm{kJ}} = 1.5
$$

So the answer is $\boxed{2.5~\mathrm{kJ},\ 1.5}$, **(a)**.
:::
:::

**P5.5 [medium].** A farmer runs a heat pump with a 2 kW motor. It should keep a
chicken hatchery at 30 °C, which loses energy at a rate of 10 kW to the colder
ambient. What is the minimum coefficient of performance that will be acceptable
for the heat pump?

![](figures/img/ch5-p-hatchery.png){width=36%}

**(a)** 2 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 5 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 3 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 1

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.hint}
At steady state, how much heat must the heat pump deliver? Not all the data given is needed.
:::

::: {.answer}
$\beta' = 5$, option **(b)**.
:::

::: {.worked}
The heat pump takes $\dot{Q}_C$ from the ambient, is driven by
$|\dot{W}| = 2$ kW, and delivers $\dot{Q}_H$ to the hatchery, which loses
$|\dot{Q}_\text{loss}| = 10$ kW to the ambient.

In order to keep the temperature constant, the heat given by the heat pump must
equal the heat losses:
$$
|\dot{Q}_H| = |\dot{Q}_\text{loss}|
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|\dot{Q}_H| = 10~\mathrm{kW}
$$

COP for the heat pump:
$$
\beta' = \frac{|\dot{Q}_H|}{|\dot{W}|} = \frac{10~\mathrm{kW}}{2~\mathrm{kW}}
= \boxed{5} \quad \text{(b)}
$$
:::
:::

**P5.6 [medium].** A sports car engine delivers 100 hp to the driveshaft with a
thermal efficiency of 25%. The specific fuel energy is 40 000 J/kg (i.e. the
energy released by burning one kilogram of fuel). Find the rate of fuel
consumption, and the combined power rejected through the radiator and exhaust.
(**Hint:** one horsepower (hp) is approximately equal to 0.735 kW.)

![](figures/img/ch5-p-sportcar.png){width=38%}

**(a)** 7.35 kg/s, 220.5 kW &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 2.67 kg/s, 220.5 kW
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 5.43 kg/s, 100.9 kW &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 9.8 kg/s, 256 kW

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.hint}
The efficiency gives the rate of heat input, and the fuel energy links that to the fuel flow. Keep the units consistent (W and J/kg).
:::

::: {.answer}
$\dot{m}_\text{fuel} = 7.35$ kg/s and $|\dot{Q}_C| = 220.5$ kW, option **(a)**.
:::

::: {.worked}
Thermal efficiency for the heat engine, with
$|\dot{W}| = 100~\text{hp} \times 735~\mathrm{W/hp} = 73\,500$ W:
$$
\eta = \frac{|\dot{W}|}{|\dot{Q}_H|}
     = \frac{73\,500~\mathrm{W}}{|\dot{Q}_H|} = 0.25
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|\dot{Q}_H| = 294\,000~\mathrm{W}
$$

The heat received in the engine is equal to the specific fuel energy times the
fuel mass flow rate, so
$$
\dot{Q}_H = \dot{m}_\text{fuel} \times 40\,000~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}}
= 294\,000~\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{s}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\boxed{\dot{m}_\text{fuel} = 7.35~\mathrm{kg/s}}
$$

From the energy equation:
$$
|\dot{Q}_C| = |\dot{Q}_H| - |\dot{W}| = 294\,000 - 73\,500
= 220\,500~\mathrm{W} = \boxed{220.5~\mathrm{kW}}
$$

So the answer is **(a)**: 7.35 kg/s, 220.5 kW. (A real fuel releases about
40 MJ/kg, a thousand times more, which would give a much more realistic
7.35 g/s.)
:::
:::
